en.title: Sleeping Dogs designer says he thinks a sequel could happen but it would need ‘a bit of planetary alignment’
en.description: It would need to be frugally developed and use its open world well, he says
en.fullContent:
It would need to be frugally developed and use its open world well, he says

A game designer who worked on Sleeping Dogs says he thinks a sequel could be possible one day, but only if a number of factors fell into place.

The original Sleeping Dogs was a 2012 open-world action adventure game published by Square Enix and developed by Canadian studio United Front Games.

The game was generally well-received and a sequel was planned but cancelled in early 2013. A online spin-off called Triad Wars was then put into development, but cancelled in late 2015 after a beta testing period.

In an interview with FRVR, Alastair Cornish – who worked as a designer on Sleeping Dogs and went on to become VP of design at Gears Tactics studio Splash Damage – says he was disappointed that Sleeping Dogs 2 was cancelled but not particularly surprised given the costs involved.

“It was super disappointing because there was a ton of space there and you’ve got a fantastic team,” he explained. “The funny thing with teams is that you’ve got to really look at where they’re positioned. Where’s the studio? What are the studio overheads? What’s the rent like?

en.title: 'More than just a cameo': New Wolverine video game features Squamish language, B.C. sites | CBC News
en.description: A sign featuring the Squamish Nation's language is on display in a new Wolverine video game that’s expected to draw millions of players globally.
en.fullContent:
A sign featuring the Squamish Nation's language is on display in a new Wolverine video game that’s expected to draw millions of players globally.

The game, Marvel’s Wolverine, will be released on Sept. 15 on PlayStation 5 and shows off several slices of B.C., including North Vancouver, the Lions Gate Bridge and the Sea-to-Sky Highway.

At one point, while the main character Logan (aka Wolverine) is driving a motorcycle along the highway, the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim (Squamish language) is displayed on two signs, spelling out the words for Whistler — Sk̲wik̲w — and Squamish — Sḵwx̱wú7mesh.

"It's something that I felt we absolutely had to do," said senior art director Gavin Goulden, who's based in Vancouver. "I worked with the team to get like the proper signage for it."

He said it was also critical to have real parts of Canada represented in the game, since Wolverine's character was born in Alberta.

"Wolverine is a Canadian hero, arguably the most famous Canadian superhero that there is," Goulden said.

en.title: Gems, ghosts and GTA VI: the biggest video games for autumn 2026
en.description: There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine ...
en.fullContent:
There are juggernauts and indie gems aplenty for when the nights draw in, from an ingenious puzzle game to blockbusters such as Marvel’s Wolverine and Call of Duty
  See all of our unmissable autumn arts recommendations here

After 20 years away, Capcom’s hyper kinetic action adventure returns, pitting skilled samurai Miyamoto Musashi against hordes of warriors and demons in Edo-period Kyoto. Master the complex combat then prepare for flashing blades, disembodied limbs and geysers of spraying blood.
  4 September; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox

Billed as the first ever 5D platformer, Screenbound has you navigating a 3D landscape while simultaneously playing an on-screen handheld console, which contains a 2D mirror world. Everything you do in one affects the other in mind-bending ways. The most ingenious puzzle game we’ve seen in a long time.
  10 September; PC, PS5, Xbox

The team behind the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man titles is back with a very different kind of hero. The open-world New York setting is gone in favour of a globe-trotting narrative following Logan on his quest to protect vulnerable mutants. The visuals are gorgeous, while the slick combat brings literal meaning to the term bleeding edge.
  15 September; PS5

The tactical role-playing adventure series returns to the realm explored in the acclaimed Fire Emblem: Three Houses. This time, hopeful contestants arrive at the glorious city of Dagsion to compete in a contest where the winner is granted a single wish. Deep combat, lush settings and fraught relationships are guaranteed.
   17 September; Switch 2

Silent Hill comes to the east coast of Scotland in a beautifully gloomy new horror adventure. You play as Simon Ordell, returning to a quiet harbour town with no memory of whatever catastrophe has taken place there. The place seems abandoned, but you are not alone for long …
  24 September; PC, PS5

en.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world
en.description: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that nee...
en.fullContent:
As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining

Predictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last week was a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to data collated by Eurogamer, more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention.

Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon.

I hope I’m wrong. I hope, at least, the BBC, which employs plenty of staff who understand video games, will make time in its schedule to take a good look at GTA VI – its themes and influences, its creators, its place in the wider culture of games and entertainment. Sure, arts coverage on BBC television has been in decline for years, with the broadcaster shifting this content to digital platforms, but I saw plenty of in-depth analysis of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, looking at the quality of its translation, its depiction of female characters, its use of practical effects. I didn’t see a single presenter shrugging, looking comedically bewildered and admitting they’d not read Homer since secondary school.

On top of this, whatever mainstream media attention GTA VI does get it will come at the expense of covering other titles. Because, when the next video game story comes up in the wake of Rockstar’s behemoth, TV and radio editors and producers will be thinking, “Oh, we covered games last month.”

The thing is, GTA is a phenomenon – it looks gorgeous, it looks vast, and it will sell many millions of copies. The series’ notoriety transcends the medium. But is it the most interesting video game since GTA V? So much has changed since then. We’ve explored the fascinating, innovative open worlds of Elden Ring, Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and No Man’s Sky (an open galaxy!); we’ve seen brutal adult themes explored in The Last of Us: Part 2 and Silent Hill; we’ve experienced dizzying narrative innovations via Disco Elysium, Split Fiction and Lost Records: Bloom & Rage. All of these deserved at least a portion of that GTA screen and radio time.

en.title: GTA 6 extended look reaches 31.1m views on Netflix in four days, making it the most-viewed title last week
en.description: The 30-minute preview was listed under Netflix's English-language films, ranking No. 1 in 87 of 93 countries tracked by the platform
en.fullContent:
The 30-minute preview was listed under Netflix's English-language films, ranking No. 1 in 87 of 93 countries tracked by the platform

The extended look of Grand Theft Auto 6  was the most-viewed title on Netflix last week, reaching 31.1 million views in four days.

As  Variety reports, viewership was tracked from the premiere last Thursday (August 27) through Sunday (August 30), which marks the end of Netflix's weekly Top 10 viewing window.

The 30-minute preview led Netflix's English-language film list in 87 of 93 tracked countries, surpassing the crime thriller The Whisper Man, which stars Robert De Niro and Adam Scott.

The premiere was exclusive to Netflix for six hours before becoming available  on YouTube. The video on Rockstar Games' channel has since reached 17 million views.

Variety noted that Netflix "defines a view as the total hours viewed for a title divided by its runtime, meaning one household watching a program twice would only be counted once." In contrast, YouTube counts a view as soon as a video begins to play.
